Are you a YouTube addict but not a fan of Google's orwellian overreach on your privacy? There is a solution and it's called Invidious.
Written By: Geovian Date: 15 October 2020

Invidious is a YouTube viewing platform that does not require you to be logged into Google. It has a number of instances that are available via a Web URL, though not all of them are active, and some instances perform better than others. I'll touch on that aspect further on.
Invidious is great when used in conjunction with De-Googled phones or on the TOR Network. You get the benefit of viewing YouTube videos but without being tracked.

One of the good things with Invidious is that you can create an account which only includes a username and a password. There is no requirement for an email nor a mobile phone number to confirm your account. So, by watching videos you can be assured that no tracking is going on.

Because there is no Google sign-in, you are unable to interact with videos by way of comments. In a way, that's actually quite a good thing as the comments section can be a feral and toxic environment.
You can however, still see all the comments, unlike the NewPipe video app which doesn't.

You do have the ability to subscribe to YouTube channels in the normal way, so you won't be missing out on your favourite vloggers. This is one of the main reasons why Invidious has an account setup, so that your subscription details are saved to it.

There are two viewing modes, the first is the traditional YouTube video layout which should be familiar to everyone, plus Invidious has its own video layout. You can select either or, and go with whatever looks right for you.

There are a handful of Invidious instances running in different parts of the world. Some work better than others. Instances are similar to federated communities, like Mastodon or Diaspora for instance.
Previously, the main instance was invidio.us, but this was closed down a few years ago as the lead developer left the project.
Here is a list of instances click on this URL
For me personally, I use the German instance invidio.xamh.de, which has all of my bases covered. I had used yewtu.be, but I noticed some glitches which prompted me to change to the German one.
For TOR users, there are several Onion links too, which you can save in your TOR browser.

Like anything to do with Google, you can expect some backlash from Big Tech in the way of obstruction or some sort of platform prevention. As at early 2022, this hasn't really happened, so enjoy the lack of overreach while we still have it.
If you're a Web Netizen, there's every likelihood that you accumulate all manner of digital information. The glue that holds it together for me is the note taking app Standard Notes.
Written By: Geovian Date: 17 October 2024

If you're a Web Netizen, there's every likelihood that you accumulate all manner of digital information. Much of it in text form. This can be in the form of website URL's which can be saved as bookmarks, or even better, saved into a web clipper app like the excellent Raindrop.io.

Or it can be a heavy collection of text files, accumulating snippets of text for any/every subject imaginable. In my case, I gather various instructions for Linux installations, not only of Linux distributions (Ubuntu, RaspberryPi, Debian etc), but also of Linux instructions to install applications and systems using a variety of methods (including Synaptic, AppImage, Flatpak etc).
The glue that holds it together for me is the note taking app Standard Notes.

This is not just any app. It can run across all platforms, and is synchronized in real time. There is no polling trigger to activate content update. You write something, as soon as you see the green tick appear in your SN page, it's updated.

The modern day problem with apps is that you cannot trust whether the developer has your best interests at heart. This is most apparent on the mobile platform. In my case, I use the Graphene OS on a Google Pixel 6a phone. All stock Android apps downloaded off the Google Playstore are quarantined (sandboxed) into their own memory/drive space on the phone, and are unable to communicate with other apps, nor "home base". All apps can have phone sensors switched off (either individually or all), meaning that apps cannot access things like the camera, the GPS etc.

Which leads me back to Standard Notes. I do use it on mobile, but have pretty much locked it down as per above. I don't bother using the specific app for Linux because it's quite clunky to set up on the command line. Plus I don't see an autostart function which I could apply using systemd scripts.
In saying that though, if you use a Distro that does still use systemd, then the autostart function works well for this apps that can take advantage of it.
I use a Debian distro (MX Linux) which doesn't use systemd anyway. So instead, I just use the web browser. A heavily locked down Brave Browser at that.
There are numerous advantages to this approach.
The data is contained in an encrypted online ecosystem, and I don't have to worry about the data should I migrate to a new laptop or even a new Linux distro. It'll all still be there.

My Brave Browser runs a Private DNS function (using AdGuard), which means no one can eavesdrop on your connection.. Brave also has a Shields option, plus I run a VPN 100% of the time (on both mobile and Linux). Call me paranoid much?

Much of the data I add into my Standard Notes store is from the web, so copy and paste is done between open Browser pages, rather than workspaces on your laptop, or different screens on mobile. I'm all for convenience.

Standard Notes direct competitor would be Evernote. The pervasive nature of Evernote's business model means I will probably never sign on with them again. I use the Standard Notes annual subscription, but you can use it for free if you so wish. It's a critical piece of my small business model toolkit, paying a sub is not an inconvenience.
Check them out at: https://standardnotes.com.

Some of you might be familiar with TOR, otherwise known as The Onion Router. For those who are unaware, TOR provides an alternative gateway onto the Internet that bypasses your Internet Providers prying eyes.
Written By: Geovian Date: 12 July 2023

Some of you might be familiar with TOR, otherwise known as The Onion Router. For those who are unaware, TOR provides an alternative gateway onto the Internet that bypasses your Internet Providers prying eyes. The objective of TOR is to provide users with a private means to surf the Internet without any bad actors unable to trace your steps back to home base. I'll explain further on.

There are a few methods and tools to enable access through a TOR Network, and after a ten year tenure of existence kicking off back in 2014, the TOR protocol has matured to the point of being able to be used as a daily driver for some.
There are a few things to note about TOR:

The TOR Protocol acts as a Proxy Server, giving you access to the Internet through a series of relays (other machines or nodes on the TOR Network which act as a bridge) to finally exit out onto the Internet (which is also known as the Clearnet) through what is known as an Exit Node. The TOR configuration generally consists of a data stream of three relay nodes at a minimum, before reaching the exit node. These three nodes help disguise your data stream, so it is mixed and tumbled with all other traffic passing through the same exit node. If it was isolated, it can only be traced back to the third last node in the chain.

In the early days circa 2014, there was just the one tool which could be used. And that was a modified version of Firefox called the TOR Browser. It was only designed to redirect web based traffic only. It could access the no-man's zone called the Dark Web. No other browser could. It was hampered by the perception of the dark web being a nefarious place, plus using the TOR Browser was very slow due to the low numbers of relay nodes on the network back then.

Then the TOR Project team rolled out Orbot, which was a one stop shop that allowed users to redirect their entire traffic to TOR. Not just web, but everything. At the time, it too was hampered by slow speeds. But looking at it again in 2024, the Orbot Service has improved out of sight. It is now much faster, with more resources and relay/nodes added to the network along with refactoring the code to improve the overall experience.
At present, Orbot is only available for Android and iOS. For PC users there are other tools out there but discussing those here is outside the scope of this post.

To clarify, Orbot is not a VPN, but it does operate similarly with a goal to anonymize traffic as much as possible. Contrary to popular belief, you cannot use Orbot and a VPN at the same time. Whoever suggested that has got their wires crossed.
Installing Orbot is easy enough. You can find it on either Appstore. Plus for Android users it's also available from F-Droid.
Setting it up is straight forward. Unfortunately I was unable to take a screenshot of the app as the app developer has put a block on it. So anyway, here the four main menu items:
Choose the Apps to be TOR Enabled, or choose VPN for entire device. VPN option is the default setting.
Change the Exit Node (leave as Global default so the exit node is always rotating)
Refresh
Turn TOR off (return to Clearnet mode).
There are other options under the More.. button below, but I'll talk about them on another day. Mostly the default settings on the first two options above will suffice.

TOR should be downloaded and kept safe as an alternate Internet gateway option. If you have a fast Internet connection, the speed should be much better. Keep an eye of the traffic meter as data passes through. It's fairly rudimentary. I'd like to see the traffic speed monitoring on the App fleshed out a little more.
In the next wee while, I'll be going down the Lokinet - Session - Nemomail rabbit hole, as Lokinet is like TOR on steroids, but it's not quite there yet. Watch this space.
It's taken years for Mozilla to land this bird onto Mobile. Finally Thunderbird (the mail client) has perched itself onto Android.
Written By: Geovian Date: 20 October 2024

I have been watching the email client space on Android for over a decade now. There's not much to tell really. most of them are good I have no problems with using them. But being a Linux devotee in that same timeframe, I had been using the Mozilla's Thunderbird mail client on both Linux and Raspberry Pi, hoping that I could one day use something similar to that on the mobile. That day finally arrived a few weeks ago.
Many people had been badgering the good people at Mozilla to create a Thunderbird email client for mobile. I remember about a decade ago this dialogue going on, so it's not a new discussion.

By 2024, the momentum had ramped up. Thunderbird development was taking off. The interesting thing is that Thunderbird is modelled heavily on the K9 Mail client. This is an obviously connection as the Thunderbird team acquired K9 back in 2022 with the intention of transitioning K9 into Thunderbird, which is what happened.

The beauty of the Thunderbird client was that it was a number of different functions all rolled into one system. We had email, a contact manager and address book, an integrated calendar, and task manager. Plus all the various plugins that could be integrated into the system.

Now in Android you can get those separate functions on separate apps. At this stage Thunderbird team have not got around to integrating all four functions into the one app. That would be a bit of work, and I'm not so sure that they'll get around to doing that anyway. as they have publicly indicated.

So the email client has landed, and the core of it is very much K9. Really, only the branding elements have changed. The Thunderbird team have relented under customer pressure and the K9 email client will still live on. There will be two ongoing development streams.
So if you use K9 or have used it, then you'll be very familiar with its appearance.

Like any good Android system, the integration across apps such as Address Book and Calendar is pretty smooth and streamlined. I also use the Ete-Sync app to keep all my emails, contacts, calendars and tasks all synchronized. I could have easily have used Google tools for this purpose but I've deliberately kept well away from Google because of their ability to dragnet one's data from their devices without their permission.

As a long time user of Thunderbird within the Linux space it's good that I finally have the same branded email client for Android even though their purposes between mobile and desktop are vastly different.

The Thunderbird team have encountered many hoops and hurdles in the development phase over the last five to ten years just in the desktop environment alone. It wasn't helped by there being so many iterations of the Android operating system (we're now up to AOSP 15.0) so just trying to find a break in the weather so to speak, was always going to be a challenge.
Thunderbird is here now for those that want to try it on your mobile. It is available on both the Google Play Store and Zapstore.

l: Australian Government - 'pie in the sky' on Encryption
p: Knowing what I know about Government, if I had my way I'd sack all Parliaments, all Governments and all public servants and we can start again from scratch.
Written By: Geovian Date: June 20, 2021
They just cannot be trusted to do the right thing on behalf of the people that they're supposed to be serving. This is definitely a case of cart before horse.

History will often show that the wrong sort of people get into power and stay there. These are not the sort of people you want to manage populations and society. Does Robert Mugabe and Zimbabwe ring a bell anyone? How about Justin Trudeau and Canada? I can see in future, that people will rise up and they will hold Governments, councils and local authorities to account.

Here in Australia, senior politicians don't really get to hang around too long, because they often get stabbed in the back by their own colleagues and next thing you know we find that a political party has a new leader, hence a new prime minister.

This is tantamount to treachery. In the last decade, we've seen Kevin Rudd, Julia Gillard, Tony Abbott and Malcolm Turnbull all depart the Prime Ministership by way of the sword. In Gillard's' case, the sword was rendered by the voting public.

Yet, the Australian Government is embroiled in more controversy. Scott (Sco Mo) Morrison is now the Prime Minister. The Home Affairs Minister Peter Dutton has more enemies than friends, and ludicrous legislation is popping out of the woodwork like termites looking for their next block of wood.

One of those legislative pieces of art is the "Telecommunications and Other Legislation Amendment (Assistance and Access) Bill 2018". After much gnashing of teeth and shouting from the rooftops, the Australian Government moved to placate the nation by ensuring that no back door decryption would be forced upon Internet Providers and other existing tools of trade.

With Google, Facebook and other Tech Giants putting tons of resources into encryption, it will be a hard sell for Government to plead their case. Though they say they are only trying to catch out the bad guys, everybody gets caught up in their Orwellian dragnet. If they can get away with it, they will.

As ZDNet Australian Editor Chris Duckett once pointed out awhile back: "The core issue is that all these schemes boil down to putting a genie back in the bottle, and to mix analogies, not only has the encrypted messaging horse bolted, but it is three paddocks over and never coming back to the stable."

China has set the bar for using technology to manage its population in a totalitarian way. The Australian Government can only dream that they too can have an overreaching system to manage its population. The problem is, they will never get there because of three things:
technology is ever-changing. Cyber security, hardened encryption and possibly blockchain.
the Australian people will not allow this to happen, over their dead bodies.
any Australian Government attempting to do this will be booted out of office.
There endth the sermon.
Modern society is so immersed in technology these days, but it doesn't take long for something to irk someone. What is your tech related pet peeve?
Written By: Geovian Date: 10 July 2020

l: It's not all that bad, isn't it?
p: Since the Internet Age took off in the late 90's, we've all been looking for the silver bullet to make our technology usage pain free and easy to use. Hasn't quite worked out that way huh? I know, having lived in the Linux Universe most of that time, the pain was severe to start out with, but has over time gotten better and better.

Some things have completely dropped off the map. Who remembers MySpace? What about Napster? Is anyone still using Pirate Bay? Actually, years later, I believe they still are. Is anyone still on a dial-up modem?

I'm not so convinced about Windows. It took two backwards steps with its development; Vista and ME being the two chief offenders. I've been off MS for many years now, though occasionally I'll have to roll out MS Word for work purposes because some clients won't deal with anything else.

How about the smart phone? I use Android mostly (a Google trap and tie-in unfortunately), I would use an iPhone but I'm not a fan of the price of their handsets nor the walled garden paradigm. Admittedly, there are more things that I like rather than dislike about phones.

What about web browsers? Is anyone still using that godawful Internet Explorer browser these days? What a crap piece of software that is. I can't believe big business still donates Microsoft millions of dollars to use their s&%$#y software. they are so last century. As for social media, I won't give them any oxygen such is my disdain, so let's not go there, haha.

So, what this demonstrates is that the 21st century adult human has had enough interactive experiences to know which things are great, productive and appealing, and which things annoy the bejeezus out of you.

What are your 5 pet peeves about technology and the overall environment in which technology pervades our lives? Here's mine. Now before I start, some of these might be minor things to a lot of people (or they could be major), usually the way to mitigate such things is to avoid them. Much like what I did with Facebook so as to avoid flame wars, for which I was a frequent contributor to. It didn't do a great deal of good to my blood pressure.

Some of the most infantile comments can be found on YouTube. Why do men (or teenage boys more than likely) have to persistently sexualize everything, even on videos where you'll find a woman talking about a completely everyday topic. The feedback from men (or boys) is just so perverse and disgusting. They wouldn't say it to her face, so they hide behind their keyboard and get their jollies that way. It annoys me no end.

I participate on a few regular boards, and you quickly discover who the chat/forum board bully is, judging by their writing style, the number of responses they make and the feedback they generate. Surely some of you have been privy to the chat/forum board bully? Ordinarily, I'd be the first one to shoot them down, but these people rise like cockroaches out of the filth. This is their way of having fun, usually at everyone else's expense. Karma is a bitch, and one day she'll come a knockin'.

If you've ever been on the Upwork site (Gig Economy Job Board), you'll notice that some job postings go from the sublime to the ridiculous. Some people post all manner of jobs, such as writing the equivalent of a Leon Uris novel all for the princely sum of $5.
Or people who say they want a 'rockstar freelancer' yet don't declare what it is they want you to do. 'Just apply and we'll advise you if you are selected'. Yeah right dumb ass!

The ones that really peeve me off are the job posters looking to rip off others web data through a process called web scraping. In most cases it's illegal, but in another word, it's technically called "theft". I hate that!

It's 2021, and web technology is such that website owners need to have two things in place. That is: SSL enabled (site encryption using https: ) and responsive HTML. Thankfully most of the major web platforms like WordPress, Laravel, Joomla etc are all responsive enabled.

However, some of the older legacy websites still don't realise that 40% of web access is done through mobile platforms now. Old wide-angled websites look like crap. So to all you website owners still living in the pre-2010 Internet, get with the program.

This mainly applies to online Newspapers. Now that physical 'paper' based newspapers are in decline. Newspaper businesses have to dream up a way to make money. They believe a paywall is that 'way', when in fact, it probably isn't.

Here in Australia, there is only one entity, that being Fairfax Media, and yet they have dozens of different regional papers, but mostly if you look on their websites, the news is all the same. Why don't they just consolidate?

If a serious media researcher was to do an analysis of where people get their news, I wonder how far up the drain pipe will a newspaper rank, ahead of Twitter, Facebook, Google News, Telegram, or other specialist sites? Probably not. I'm sure newspapers will be relevant for some time yet, but not pay walls. However, it does make for great fish and chip wrapping.
What are your pet peeves? Drop us a line in the Comments section below.

The Internet back-chatter is all a flurry at the moment about the current version of the Internet potentially closing down completely and replaced by something new. A bit of a doomsday scenario I know but what if, it did go down, then what happens to your data wherever it is stored?
Written By: Geovian Updated: 5 November 2024

I won't get into the whys and wherefors about the Internet potentially shutting down, that's a discussion for another day and beyond the scope of this article. Having a backup strategy for your all-important data, whether stored on the cloud or stored in a web host database for your public facing website is the issue here. Let's go over a few of the issues.

When the Cloud strategy came in to play a few years ago, Enterprises more so than small business thought it was the next best thing since sliced bread. I've always been dubious about Cloud services, because I knew at the end of the day if the cloud went belly up or was hacked, my data was compromised. I always wanted to ensure my data was safe under my own roof, so to speak.

Also, not all businesses were convinced. For those that had security oriented data, like intellectual property (software code for instance), then putting it up on the cloud was a no-go. Unless stringent clauses were included under a service level agreement (SLA). However, one of the benefits of using a cloud service is that all the technology, skills, expertise and resources available through an outsourced arrangement, for a price of course.

For our readership/audience, technology will play a part in a small business operation for sure, but I'm guessing probably not to the same level as a corporate Enterprise using a data warehouse for instance. So therefore, being able to backup your data might be an easier proposition than you realise.
Let's say that you have a WordPress website. Ok, fairly common but there are two aspects to it as there is with any website infrastructure, and that is:
your content (data, records etc)
your entire website infrastructure minus the content.

Using the example above with WordPress, the content aspect is straight forward. WP posts might be loaded up directly on the web page, or if like me, you can create it in a document or text file offline and just copy and paste it on to the Web page or FTP up to the appropriate directory on your Web server. That way you have an offline copy immediately.

The second part is the infrastructure, and this is where it gets tricky, unless you are very familiar with dealing with content management systems, plugins, uploading of images, and all that stuff. Notwithstanding, some business owners don't bother with uploading their own version of a content management system, instead they use a service like Softaculous which your web host will automatically install for you on your Web domain hosting plan.

Despite all this, when creating a website part of your planning process should include a continuity of operation strategy. Which quite simply means having the ability to restore your website from scratch in case something untoward happens. And by 'scratch', this means you have access to your up-to-date content and infrastructure in an offline capacity, so that such a restore can take place without relying on the vagaries of a cloud backup. My motto simply is:
"if your data is not in your direct hands then it's not in your control."

In one of my situations, I have had web data online since 1999, and I am absolutely anal about saving the content offline at all times. Never have I had to worry about losing any of it because I've got it backed up in different places both online and offline in case of emergencies. Some might consider it to be a little bit paranoid, but it gives me peace of mind and more importantly I know that it will save me money in the long run if a full blown restore is required. Losing 22 years of content is not to be contemplated. As it is, I have the technical capabilities to do it myself but that's something other small business owners might not be able to do.

l: Using Google, Wix and other free services
p: Despite what people will tell you about free services, the reality is, they are not really free. There is always a cost whatever that might be, hidden in the packaging. So, if you are using a free service like Google, Wix, Zoho, please ensure at the very least you have the capability to backup your data to an offline repository. Yes, at the very least.

I will ask the same question about email, uploading of images and other content you've placed up onto the cloud, like Facebook, Instagram or Tiktok or whatever. Sure some of these tools are very useful to the layperson, and I have no problem with that. The problem then becomes: 'what happens when you're not able to get access to your data, let's say if the Internet goes down or if there's a long outage of some sort and your business requires access to your data.

Many people and many business owners have different strategies on how to manage their data. Some of them have super strong bulletproof strategies, but I'll go out on a limb and say that 80% have a strategy that is totally and utterly inadequate, and that they are ill-prepared for a tech catastrophe if and when it happens. A very sobering thought.

The robustness of your continuity of operation strategy depends on how serious you are about preserving your data. If you have a cavalier attitude about it all then you probably shouldn't be reading this page. If you are concerned, read on.

We've discussed web data above. If you are outsourcing your web services work to someone else, have a talk to them about a backup strategy. It is your data after all, don't accept no for an answer. Get it documented, and include it in your overall business plan for transparency purposes.
It depends on how and where your email is being used. There are four typical categories:
public email service (Gmail, Hotmail, Yandex, GMX).
a corporate email attached to a business (maybe you're employed there).
your own mail hosted on your own hosted domain.
email hosted on your own server privately, say at home (setup and configuration is not for the faint hearted).

The first two categories do not give you a great deal of flexibility to download your email data. However, you could use a Microsoft Outlook client in hooking into any mail services and then save your email to what is called a PST file which is located locally on your computer. I haven't used Outlook for many years so I'd need to come up to speed with that type of solution.

The Mozilla mail client called Thunderbird is another option, but you need to configure your t-bird mailboxes to download content directly onto your computer. This can be done, but the file size of your mailboxes might get quite high if you send out lots of mail and also mail with attachments. Better to have them locally than not I say. Note: Thunderbird is only available for the Desktop.

The third category can also be saved onto a local computer. No problem there. Its what I do. You'd probably need to set it up using a POP3 port rather than IMAP, but do test the ability to download to your computer because not all mail clients are the same. Simply switch off your internet for a moment, go into your mail client and see if you can read the content of the emails intact when offline. If so, it works.

The fourth category is for those who are more than technically capable of setting up their own public facing servers at home including the provision of a mail server. If so, your data is 100% online but also 100% offline, if that makes sense. Again, that might be a discussion for another day.

Calendars are normally attached to an email address, as with Gmail. Tasks are also included into Calendars. So when migrating calendars through a CALDAV server, both Calendar and Tasks data will come across. With a bit of configuration, you can point nearly any calendar client or app, to other online repositories such as Google, EteSync, Nextcloud, Calendarly or Teamup. Make sure you can save your entries offline.

This is a hairy one because contributions to social media are considered by many to be of a throwaway nature. And because social media belongs to someone else, the question arises as to whether or not your contributions are worth saving, notwithstanding whether your contributions can actually be saved offline, then restored back onto someone else's system (like Facebook), it then begs the question, can it be done? My initial thoughts on that would probably lean towards 'no', you won't be able to.

If you use an image library service (like having an account on imgur), does that mean you have all of your images saved offline as well? I hope you do and I assume that you do. If not, make it happen.

The best, easiest and cheapest backup strategy for your data is to use a USB hard drive attached to your desktop or laptop, or a higher specced NAS Drive attached to your home WIFI system as network detectable device via IP Addressing. Anything over 4tb will not cost an arm or a leg. I have two Western Digital USB drives: one is a 4tb drive, the other a smaller 500gb drive. All of my content data lives on there. If worst comes to worst, like a house fire or some such, I can quickly grab them and depart the house using my Home Evacuation Procedure.
If any of you have your own backup solution that works for you and consider it might be useful for others, then hook up and drop in comment below.

Like many, I've had enough virtual intrusion from the likes of Fakebook, Google, Twitter, and many other big tech players. So some of us are doing something about it. We're going back to the future: going old school.
Written By: Geovian Updated: 5 November 2024

Remember at the start of the century? Nokia was king. Before all this intrusion and surveillance nonsense took over. If you look at technology today, I believe there are three ways to manage your digital life where you control the virtual narrative, and no one else.
we move all of our context back under our own virtual roof where it can't be interfered with. Usually to an offline repository of your choice.
keep it in the cloud under your own strict control, like an encrypted Nextcloud instance hosted on your own domain.
or, move it to a trusted de-centralized and federated platform where no single person or entity has the power to boot you off, or de-platform you.
Personally, I would aim up at options 1 and 2.
OK, let's now take a look at the lay of the land, in particular around the use of mobile networks and smartphones.

Have you seen the prices for the new mobile phones in particular those offerings from Apple and Samsung? The prices are really off the scale. No sane person would spend over 2000 bucks for a new phone. From those two manufacturers even if you took their flagship phones from 3 to 4 years ago they are still well over the thousand dollar range.

To me, this suggests a brainwashed and captive market for those people who need the comfort and satisfaction of being one step ahead of everyone else. That is ego-centric thinking at its best (or worst). Who the fuck cares?
Yes phones are still important as communication devices, but now more than ever, we should only allow the flow of dialog in one direction mostly; that being outwards and not inwards.

Unless you are paranoid and have blacklisted everything on your phone, the modern smartphone allows all manner of communication and data to flow from your phone, and in many cases leaving your phone without your knowledge! Android and iOS apps are the main instigators of our concern here.

l: Can we go back to old style phones?
p: To ensure Google can't get to you on your phone, you could always return to an older style phone, like an older styled Nokia handset. Some of these phones are not powered by Android which means they are not supplemented by Google. The only things you can do are to make phone calls and to send SMS. The basis of an old style phone right?

Unfortunately, one of the problems is that these phones use older Telco networks, like CDE or GSM, many of which have been deprecated around the world. Most phones these days are running 3G 4G and 5G.

In this current era of CoronaVirus and lockdown, it's a good idea to be off the Internet anyway, so you avoid all the fake news going on across News Sites and Social Media, but unfortunately, too many people are addicted to tech in the most unhealthiest of ways.
Anything that doesn't have direct hooks back to Google (which also includes YouTube, Microsoft, Fakebook and Twitter/X would be a good thing. In this regard, a Linux distro is ideal.

So you want to do Internet stuff. Well don't do it on a phone if you are really paranoid, but do it on a small form factor device like a Raspberry Pi and a touchscreen monitor. RPi handles Linux distros like a boss, though do remember that only ARM based distros can be installed on a Pi. A single board computer (SBC) like the Odyssey X86 can run x86 Linux builds, whereas the RPi as mentioned runs ARM builds only. Either way, good choices, but I'd opt for the RPi because of the better support and distribution.

How about installing a custom ROM like Lineage or Calyx? Unfortunately this is easier said than done, as the entire procedure is not for the faint hearted. It involves a number of steps including rooting your phone, finding the right custom ROM that matches your phone (say Lineage OS), and then there's the tricky procedure of overriding your existing Android build with the custom one. Many a phone has been bricked by attempting to install a custom ROM with disastrous consequences. You should only ever attempt this if you truly know what you are doing.

As at late 2021, Linux phones are now a thing, though in its infancy and still not mature enough to be a viable proposition. So, devices like the PinePhone and Librem5 are the best known of this new brigade but they have a long way to go before reaching mass acceptance let alone a breakeven point.
Let's not forget that 2022 is supposed to be the year of the Quantum phone, or so we've been told. We'll be keeping an eye on that space for sure. Step on up Elon Musk.

I'll focus on mobile rather than a home broadband setup because mobile is where Google has aimed up at consumers due to the ease in which they extract your data via Android. So this is the platform where most of the privacy effort needs to be applied.

A VPN is important, if only to disguise your online activity and to throw the bloodhound off the scent, so to speak. Choosing a VPN is an art in itself. Don't rely on online reviews as most of the people writing them up are being paid to do so by the VPN company itself!

Some people swear by TOR, though it is tricky to configure, especially in the area of proxies, bridges and endless Captcha screens. If you can get past these three things, and unlearning some bad habits of online surfing from your recent past, then TOR might be a possibility for you.

Private DNS is now a thing. This can be applied to all modern Android phones uding Android 13 or higher, both at the phone level or st the browser level (like Brave). Or even both! Choose between the Adguard or Cloudflare solution. My preference is Adguard.

Possibly a DNS Resolver and Anominizer might provide some help. Cloudflare have a DNS tool which is useful, though I'd be loathe to use Google's DNS of 8.8.8.8. That's just inviting trouble. I'll write more about DNS in a future article, including a newish Android app currently in beta called Rethink DNS.

If you are torrenting, it's essential that you use a VPN to disguise your real world IP address, and also to use a Torrent client which forces encryption on both the download and upload channels. Most do, but it pays to check in your client settings anyway. This provides two forms of obfuscation when your disguised IP address is presented to the torrent file swarm as a tracker.

And finally, if you are one of those people who surfs naked around the Internet mostly on a smartphone, then you definitely need to install a No Root Firewall on your device, to prevent Google and other Big Tech companies from pinging your device and taking YOUR data. Once installed it's easy to set up and easy to switch off all apps and services from communicating with home base, and only allow those by whitelisting. ET phone home? Not in this case.

Note: Unfortunately you cannot use No Root Firewall alongside an existing VPN app that you have on your phone. All smartphones have a single VPN Port so you can't have two applications running on one port.
Search for No Root Firewall on the Play Store, F-Droid or an APK repository like Aptoide.
There you go, some food for thought.
Trying to make sense of the gobbledegook of job vacancy ads.
Written By: Geovian Date: 13 October 2024

I'm sure many of you have undertaken the unholy task of reading through and applying for jobs online through various job broker services. Unfortunately applying for jobs in this manner is an unfortunate byproduct of the employment industry.
If you are lucky enough to be self-employed and to generate your own income without having to be saddled with the job application process, then lucky you.

Due to changes in the workforce landscape across all industries, the job application process is becoming a lot more difficult because of the circumstances around remote work/being in the office, retrenched businesses, roles being overtaken by technology automation and AI, lack of a career pathway and reduction in salary.

Not helping matters are the requests laid out by employers and their recruitment agencies when it comes to the recruitment process. You can read the nonsense they write up in their job ads. Much of it is corporate speak, where they use jargon, corporate terminology that only they know about and the use of obscure acronyms, without explaining what they are, and expecting you to know what it means.
Much of these job adverts have been written by rank amateurs with no true idea of how to put a proper job ad together.

In some cases, roles for company positions have transitioned from one era to another without any change being made to the position description. You could be applying for a job in the 2000s but the job description reads like it was written for someone back in the 1970s. In my experience, privately held companies suffer from this malaise more than government departments, who at least do a better job of keeping roles/positions updated.
Now with online job portals being the go-to place to finding a new job, you can now go in with a better understanding of what they require just by doing a careful analysis of their job advert.
Let's take a look at some gotchas.
So what does this mean when you first come across this term? Is 'fast paced' a good thing, and if so how and why? Is it indicative of a chaotic environment?

Surely that wouldn't be a good thing? You'd be surrounding yourself with people running around like chooks with their heads cut off. Goodness no, I've seen that often enough. Be brave enough to ask, and observe the response.

l: No one day is similar to the other
p: This is another phrase that annoys the bejeezus out of me. Of course this depends on what type of job is up for grabs. At face value though, what it suggests borders on a state of regular chaos throughout the working week.

The flight plan for your job is your job description. Hopefully your line manager will understand this. If not, you're in trouble. Lol. If you see this phrase or something similar, it's best to put the interviewer on the spot.

This would rank as one of the dumbest statements you can read on a job application. Unless you have the skills of an Nostradamus or a Madam Blatva with a crystal ball, 'passion' is an empty piece of verbiage made to sound more impressive than it actually is.
And besides, how can you have passion for a job which you haven't even landed yet? How can you even quantify that word, or its twin 'passionate? Marks out of 10? Zero.

Now I've seen this phrase pop up more often than not. It normally applies to senior or managerial roles, but equally lower level job ads also include this. Why do companies want to put the equivalent of a brick wall in their job ads?

For some prospective employees, this is a red rag to a bull. In other words, stress could imply disorganization, ineffective application of resources including staffing, processes and procedures not being adhered to, technology failure and interpersonal conflict. All resulting in corporate chaos.
Defining 'stress' within the confines of both the job and the company should be identified so you know what you're dealing with from day one.
Well this all very flowery and pompous, not on the least subjective as well, and totally irrelevant to put in a job ad.

There is a saying that goes "beauty is in the eye of the beholder". In this case, the beholder won't actually know if the applicant is talented and motivated until they've actually been appointed to the role. So what's the point of actually putting it into a job ad before you appoint anyone?

Surely the company won't be dumb enough to ask that question in an interview? Not only would it be inappropriate but it would be totally unethical. A sure sign for the interviewee to "run to the hills".

If you read hundreds of job adverts online you'll soon discover some of the most overly used buzzwords that try to make the job a little bit more attractive than it probably is in real life. Here's a few:
Passion - yes that word again, employers please delete this word from your vocabulary.

Innovative - if you've been in a job long enough you'll find ways to become innovative through continuous improvement and familiarity. Take that as a given, it doesn't need to be mentioned in a job ad.

Prioritize - if you are a perfectly functioning adult, you'll know what prioritizing is in your day-to-day life. Nothing changes from your domestic life to your work life. Humans know how to prioritize, take it as a given too. I believe this is another vacuous term of no importance.

enthusiastic - well this is all rather subjective and it depends on what type of job is being advertised. Try putting this in an ad for a cleaner or a janitor. Throwing it around willy-nilly in a job ad means that it's likely to be a filler word more than most.

offer professional growth - I've seen this term used in job ads that are so low quality and so low paying, that even burger flippers in McDonald's earn more. The old adage applies: you get what you pay for.

Attention to detail - why do companies put terms like this in their ads? This suggests to me that companies who are advertising like this are expecting people to apply who don't exhibit these traits. And during the interview process, how would they know anyway? This reads like a disingenuous term which could be reworded in a more friendlier tone.
I'm sure there are many other examples, but I've just picked on a couple that have sprung up over the last couple of days which made me mad enough (or annoyed enough) to write something about it.

But, I can guarantee you that when you next read a job advert online, you'll see some of these terms being repeated ad nauseum. It just goes to show that some of these recruitment companies in line with their corporate clients are reading off the same repetitive page year after year. It's getting boring.
So, if you are preparing for a job interview go well prepared with questions at the ready. Use this as a guide. Good luck.

How do you know when you've collected too many tech toys? If you don't toss them out, does that mean you're a hoarder? Lol.
Written By: Geovian Date: 22 September 2023

I'm sure that many of us have collected tech gadgets over the years and kept hold of them for one reason or another. Whether it be computers, laptops, routers, printers, old smartphones, clunky hard drives. You name it. Many would say it's an emotional attachment. Others remember how much some of these things cost when they were first bought, so getting rid of them is a bitter pill to swallow because you're not getting any financial compensation for something that is of no use anymore - which in effect is another emotional response.
For those that don't have an emotional attachment to such things then kudos to you.

Attachments to physical objects comes in many forms. For me, it was old LP's and CD's. I amassed a huge collection, and it followed me around the world whenever or wherever I moved house. Decades later I wondered why I bothered. Thank you Spotify.

Yes, breaking the chains of attachments can be hard, but conversely, keeping hold of such things also acts as an anchor. Physical inanimate objects are nothing more than 'things'. My way of thinking is this. If it's not going to be important in 5 or 10 years time, then don't place any emotional value on it. Move on. There are more important things to concern yourself with.

I knew some people who hoarded stuff obsessively. Years ago I used to do part time work as a Census Collector, some of the houses I saw both inside and out defied belief. From piles of old newspapers racked miles high to properties with rusted cars and car parts making an auto wreckers yard look trivial. I could never understand it.

Looking back I too was guilty of hoarding tech gear, thinking it might get reused on some IT restoration project which never eventuated. Boxes of ethernet and USB cables, peripherals, power supplies, old phones and routers were stashed in wardrobes never to see the light again. What was the point? It was always easier to buy the latest gadget but as a result, the unused hoarded pile just kept getting bigger.

These days tech is a bit more streamlined but in 5 to 10 years time we'll probably be questioning our current consumer choices and wondering why we bothered with some of them. It's called the price of progress, and our trail of consumerism over the years is evidence of that progress even if it meant discarding tech along the way as it became out of date.
So, if you have a few hours to spare on a lazy Sunday afternoon, perhaps it's time to have a clean out? I'm sure your spouse will be overjoyed.

l: Work From Home - The New Normal?
p: You can thank the COVID response and forced lockdowns for demonising the global workforce into 'working from home', a term now abbreviated to WFH.
Written By: Geovian Date: 17 October 2021

Remote working (another earlier name for WFH) had been in vogue for many years prior to the dubious 2020 outbreak, and for me personally, I've been doing WFH since 2004. It's taken 15 plus years for the rest of the world to catch on.

So what do today's modern workforce need to understand about their professional responsibilities to their job and employer? Conversely, what do employers need to do to ensure continuity of their workforce under these forced new arrangements? Let me go over a few pointers - talking from someone with 15 years of experience.

l: Don't take the situation for granted
p: As of mid-2021, the world is not quite ready for a complete migration to WFH. Maybe in the near future when industry is convinced that productivity and profitability is not compromised by having a remote workforce will it become the rule rather than the exception.

Mostly, I believe it's more of a trust issue that employers need to overcome. Nowadays, skilled professionals can pick and choose their roles, and if the job can be undertaken from a home office, you can bet many people will apply. Going to the office, sitting in traffic and putting up with the corporate BS that goes on in every workplace is a huge turnoff to many. There are plenty of available jobs out there and not enough people to fill them.

Of course, working from home is made easier now because of the global situation. Social distancing in particular and offices being forced to close to prevent the spread of the so called virus are but two of the principle reasons why. Err hmm, cough cough..

But that's not to say productivity isn't compromised. People all operate differently and whereas some will struggle with WFH (especially those that need to feel the vibe of fellow workmates around them), there are others who will absolutely enjoy the solitude, allowing them to zone in on the work with minimal disruption.
Here are several pointers that WFH employees should follow to be productive:
Be professional, even if you'd love to be dressed in your Pj's and slippers while on a Zoom call.
Ensure your home office is equipped with all the tools you require to do the job.

A reliable Internet connection is a must. In Australia where I live, speeds have dropped to third world levels. It is simply appalling. We are all waiting for Elon Musk to put more Starlink satellites up in the sky and bring down the entry cost of that service.
Stay in touch regularly with your coworkers, whether by phone, email, online chat or Zoom call. Don't get lost out in the 'Burbs.

Get out and exercise when you can. Just because you're at home doesn't mean you should become a recluse and a coach potato. Try to avoid a sedentary lifestyle. Your health will thank you for it. Trust me I know.
If you're working on the clock, organise yourself to be prompt and to be available. Absence arouses suspicion if your coworkers are none the wiser as to your whereabouts.

If you're only being paid for a 40 hour week, then work those 40 hours. Not 60 or 80. Just because you're at home and it's convenient doesn't mean you should pick up some bad timekeeping habits. You won't get paid any extra.

Avoid distractions. This is a biggie. Avoid social media, personal correspondence or other non-work related activity, like a side hustle for instance. Remember, you're on company time. Respect the privileged position you are in.

Not all employers are the same. What works for one company won't work for another. However, don't be closed minded by wanting the situation to return to the way how things used to be pre Covid. The world has moved on and the employment industry has changed significantly from two years ago.

Employees now have many other priorities going on in their lives. For example, working for an employer that demands getting the jab is enough for that employee to resign and walk away, while prospective employees could thumb their noses and look elsewhere if presented with that challenge. Yes, personal health is a priority, and not everyone believes in the government narrative, which is so full of holes and laden with fear mongering.

Don't be surprised if there is very little interest in your vacancies. Many job adverts are poorly written, full of cliches, rhetoric and corporate jargon. People can spend less than a minute glossing over an advert and know immediately that they'll pass on it. Employers really need to lift their game if they want to attract top talent. Offering a WFH option could be one incentive, but it shouldn't be the only one.

If an employer absolutely demands a 9 to 5 work day located at the office, they should also look at online case studies of people who currently do WFH, or those who have done it for years, and maybe learn something about the changing landscape around this concept called 'work/life balance', because it isn't a myth.

Remember that employees have a life outside of work too, and that a job is just that. People come and go all the time, and they simply will not commit to your organisation as a one-company employee, as those days have gone.

In some cases, a WFH opportunity is the No #1 priority for people, as issues to do with family, health, childcare, home schooling, and unnecessary time spent in traffic all present challenges which can be alleviated by working from home.

In the 21st century, times are indeed changing. Not everyone wants to work for someone else, or work in an office. The younger generation are disrupters and game changers, and would prefer to run their own businesses.

Why? Because firstly, they've seen from observing their parents and grandparents what an unrewarding experience it was for them to be a part of the workforce back then, and secondly, they are more driven to succeed than compared to previous generations.
Being able to do all this working from home is the icing on the cake.

Do you have a flash state of the art phone? Do you want it to be your first device of choice and to be able to use it as your laptop too? Then read on.
Written By: Geovian Date: 10 April 2021

For far too long the business world has lived in a duopoly environment of mobile phones and computers - be it desktops, laptops and tablets. From my perspective it's an incredible waste of money, not forgetting the huge amounts of E-waste that is created every year.

Having seperate devices back in the early days was definitely warranted, as mobile phone specifications were very basic, certainly not as sophisticated as they are today. However, the perceived gap between the usage on a state of the art mobile versus a laptop for instance - is being bridged slowly but surely. One of the mobile phone's features that is helping pave the way is a bit of functionality in the Google/Android space, it's something called Desktop Mode.

This feature has been around for a little while, but has been given very little love by the software Engineers at Google. It is part of the Android ecosystem including the latest version 11 but really Google is asking for the phone manufacturers to take the functionality already there and improve upon it with a bit of spit and polish on their own flagship phones.

There are also some software developers that are building Linux distros that can interface with compatible 'desktop-mode enabled phones. An example being Maru OS which is exclusively interfacing with Google's Nexus brand of phones at the moment, but the lead developer there says the intention is to interface with all Android phones, which sounds like a bit of a stretch, particularly for older phones.

The phone manufacturers which have led the charge include Samsung, Huawei and LG, while Oppo and Xiaomi have also jumped onboard with at least one of their phones being desktop-mode enabled. Future builds of phones are expected to include desktop-mode by default, though phone manufacturers that triple up as laptop, tablet and chromebook manufacturers may be initially cautious, as they could cannibalize their own market share for those products.

l: So anyway, what does Desktop-Mode do?
p: So long as you have a compatible phone that can run desktop mode, the idea is to connect your phone to a portable monitor that acknowledges phones via HDMI at one end, paired with a device that has a USB-C port at the other end.

Not only can you connect a phone to a portable monitor to get a bigger (or even second separate) screen, you can also connect a game console or even a RaspberryPi to the portable monitor because those ecosystems support desktop mode too. In the Samsung universe we are talking Samsung Dex, with Huawei they call theirs Easy Projection while LG's is simply LG Desktop Mode.

I have never used Samsung Dex but some people I know around the world swear by it and started putting their laptops and desktops into retirement. Being able to use your phone and two different modes definitely has some advantages. If you're working on large spreadsheets and PowerPoint presentations, these are things that you can blast out onto a bigger screen more so than you could do on a phone. That's only one efficiency, there are many more.

The Internet is home to a dime a dozen selection of devices such as portable monitors, whether you buy on Amazon, eBay or AliExpress, there's something there for everybody. However, with desktop mode you'll need to be a little bit more prudent in your selection, as there are some features you'll need to consider.

Most decent monitor manufacturers include a dual power supply option with two connection jacks. One for the standard 12v connection to the wall (country specific) as well as a 5v USB-C connection to a battery bank. The latter would mean you could supply battery bank power to both your phone and RaspberryPi for instance plus the monitor, all the while without impacting on your electricity bill. An excellent option for The Great Outdoors too, but only if you can get guaranteed mobile phone service.

It goes without saying, a portable monitor is the ultimate portability solution for that busy executive who needs to be productive on the road but without sacrificing any of the tools that he would use in the office. If you purchase a suitable portable monitor then usually it will come with a carry case. Probably the other things you might need is something like a kickstand and a lapdesk, which is just a foldaway table that you can sit yourself underneath whether on the couch or sitting up in bed, this would be your work bench.

My own personal opinion is that a touch screen and portable monitor go hand in hand. A hand fits glove arrangement. I couldn't comprehend using one without touchscreen being enabled. But at the end of the day it all depends on what the manufacturer specifications are for its touchscreen as well as the price. The price can certainly vary, so you do need to do some homework and selective shopping before you hand over your hard earned cash.

Written By: Geovian Updated: 10 Deceember 2024

Here's a quick explainer as to how we set up Private DNS for both your mobile device and your browser. Private DNS as an innovative piece of security technology is relatively new. It's been around in various guises since around 2016 or 2017 but nowadays has developed to be an important part of an internet users privacy and security toolkit.

In this regard, we're talking mainly about ads in the prevention of ads showing up in places like Facebook, YouTube, X and all the other social media haunts. Coupled with that, are invasive tracker codes that can follow you around the Internet like a homeless dog.
An example of a tracker code is one that's found on a YouTube url if you copy a video onto your phone or computer.
https://youtube.com/watch?v=3TpSoR189Wo&pp=ygUPVGVycmEgZGVsIGZ1ZWdv

If you didn't know any better you'd copy the whole URL onto one of your own web pages and be none the wiser for the code that you've just embedded with tracking on it. Just strip out anything after the &pp code.

Not only that, but corporate websites are also mining your user data through cleverly concealed ads that they put on their web pages through images, icons and hidden links. Filling out online forms is particularly dangerous, especially if financial information is required. Always err on the side of caution, because surreptitious harvesting is always happening.

To help mitigate some of these threats, some companies in the cyber security space have enabled technology to shut down ads and privacy threats without the need to add multiple extensions into your browser. Private DNS is one of these, and when combined with a reputable VPN, you have the makings of good operational security in place.
At this time, there are four major players in the Private DNS space:
Cloudflare
Quad 9
Adguard
OpenDNS

I have not used OpenDNS. I have used Cloudflare and Quad 9 but I found that they don't fully encrypt the connection on a consistent basis. I have frequented a number of sporting websites that have a lot of ads on them, so I can tell when Private DNS is working properly or not. The only one that consistently works time and again is Adguard. The ads disappear.

Remember though that websites are playing a game of whack-a-mole. So they will change their code or find ways to try and circumvent Private DNS. But from what I've seen so far and reading all of the literature from places like Reddit and other tech security type websites, is that many of these harvesters have been unsuccessful. So that's a good thing.
So, we'll focus on Adguard as this is definitely a good option for mobile users and computer users. For this article I'll focus only on the mobile platform.
Before we get started, Adguard have put up a page which identifies all of the devices and platforms where Private DNS is supported.
click here There are instructions for the iPhone, but because I don't use Apple products I'll focus on Android for this particular article.
Enable Private DNS:\
Go to Settings > Network & Internet >
Advanced > Private DNS.
Toggle the switch to enable Private DNS. Choose AdGuard DNS:\
Select the “Private DNS provider hostname” option.
Enter dns.adguard.dns.com as the hostname.
Click Save to lock it in. Configure DNS-over-TLS:\ Since Android 13 only supports DNS-over-TLS (DoT), you won’t need to configure any additional settings. There is nothing more for you to do here.
[Note:] AdGuard Private DNS can work alongside a third party VPN or you can use Adguard's own VPN so that the two products can work alongside each other.

[Note 2:] Private DNS was introduced into the Android operating system via the Android 13 update. If you have an old phone you'll need to see if it's original manufacture and software install are either before or after Android 13. All modern phones going back at least 5 years should be compatible.

on your Brave Browser, click the three dot menu, and go to the Settings option.

If you're using your mobile phone for writing and editing, then s virtual keyboard is essential. Some are better than others, including the excellent Heliboard.
Written By: Geovian Date: 17 March 2025
I belong to several cyber security sites on various platforms. There, they talk about the various apps and solutions that they use to improve their operational security, otherwise known as OPSEC.
The three key takeaways that I've picked up through these platforms are:
open source
encryption and
zero cost (free)
Finding something that has all three is like landing the holy grail. Finding something that has at least two of those things is like landing the jackpot.

So it is with the excellent virtual keyboard Heliboard. Now, it would be fair to say that I've used a number of different virtual keyboards in my time. All of them have come with some form of caveat. With Google and Microsoft keyboards, you can easily understand what those caveats will be. Lack of privacy and data vacuuming.
Trying to find a virtual keyboard without compromising your OPSEC ethics turned out to be a long wait. Bit Heliboard was worth it. Let's get down to the nitty gritty.

Heliboard takes its origins from the Openboard project, built for the Android Open Standards Project (AOSP). It was forked to become Heliboard. In doing so the app retained being an open source project plus its existence is purely offline. No phoning home to big mama, which is great for privacy enthusiasts.

As far as the app itself is concerned, there is a lot of technical setup to be done, but at the end of it, the results are quite impressive. Firstly, there are three themes that you can apply to Heliboard. These are: Material, Holo and Rounded.

Secondly, there are numerous color options that you can apply to the keyboard and the elements surrounding it. Under the Appearance you can apply the preloaded color templates, Or you can do what I did and that is to use the custom design template and come up with your own random selection of colors for the keyboard background.

Thirdly, you can add the emoji option as well as the number toolbar across the top like most other virtual keyboards have. Every character key will have a long press option that you can use to apply alternative character strokes.

Fourthly, you will have to add in a plugin to activate voice to text input. This will be via the Futo Voice Input Method which you can download from Zapstore or F-Droid. Once downloaded and installed, you can then set it up and link it to the Heliboard app.

The Futo app is visible in the top toolbar via the microphone icon. At least being placed here at the top rather than being placed inside the comma character key (as it was on the Microsoft Swift keyboard) means that it is safely out of the way.

Having most recently worked with Microsoft's Swift keyboard, I had to get used to some configuration changes regarding the placement of character keys and also to the design of emoji characters. These are mostly cosmetic in nature.

One of the things that appears to be missing which I found quite valuable on the Microsoft Swift keyboard is the ability to backspace and hold down the delete key and know that it would just delete the word in question without taking out a whole bunch of other characters preceding it, that is if you held the delete key down for too long. I've had a look in the settings to see if there is something to manage this, but it doesn't look like it.
Overall Heliboard is a very useful addition to the OPSEC toolkit as s virtual keyboard, and one that meets the criteria of zero cost, open source and privacy.

We're midway through 2024 and things are starting to heat up in the Starlink space.
Written By: Geovian Date: July 21 2024

[Originally written in 2020] For those of you who don't know what Starlink is, listen up. You know who Elon Musk is right? The guy and his company Tesla are behind such innovations as Tesla Battery Banks, Tesla cars, the Space X rocket program and also the Starlink Satellite service for global Internet. That's right. Global Internet, going head to head with land based giants such AT&T, Verizon, Vodafone, Bell, British Telecom (BT), Telstra and many others.

Space X and Starlink is guaranteed to be a game changer, in that their coverage will reach hard to access locations around the globe, and be able to increase transmit speeds well beyond the terrestrial levels we see now. Many disadvantaged people in remote locations will now have faster access speeds than those more affluent and tech savvy slickers living in the cities. How ironic. The average download speeds are over 200mb per second, while upload speeds are around 50mbps. These speeds completely blows away 3G, 4G and 5G speeds, making them just about obsolete.

Being an Australian resident, I am particularly interested to see what the impact of Starlink will be on consumers outside of the Metropolitan regions of our vast nation, and what this will mean for those in rural areas and of course those living in the Outback.

Space X had to seek permission from the Australian Government to obtain a license to deliver its services into Australia. Initially, this was going to be to rural and Outback areas only, with the Metropolitan regions being prohibited mainly because the Australian Government has a vested interest in the NBN scheme, as in the National Broadband Network scheme, for which it has invested millions of dollars already.

I suspect that if Starlink was made available to Metro regions it would kill off the NBN in double quick time, even if Elon Musk says that Starlink at this point in time is better suited to low population densities such as rural and outback areas. Despite this statement, I am certain that it will not stop Internet obsessives living in Australian cities to sign up if and when it becomes officially available. Hopefully by then, Space X and Starlink would have put more satellites up in the sky, interconnectivity between them will have improved, so too the technology to make it all happen.

In telecommunications speak, Metropolitan areas around the six largest Australian cities (Melbourne, Sydney, Brisbane, Gold Coast strip, Adelaide and Perth) are zoned specifically. Everything else is zoned as Area 74. When Space X/Starlink were first issued a license to operate by the Australian Communications and Media Authority (ACMA), it was issued for Area 74 only.

However, in recent weeks, it appears that some users inside the metro zones are getting coverage, as reported by Australian industry observer Chris Vanderstock on his YouTube channel. Whether this is a technical glitch on Starlink's part or whether this is an undocumented feature - we are none the wiser at this point.

Yes, there is a bit of science involved, and it revolves (excuse the pun) around the curvature of the planet, the best orbital paths for satellites to travel and how far up in the sky the satellites are positioned.

Starlink global coverage is not equitable no matter where you are on the planet. Some locations will be better off than others. For instance, there is no coverage for either polar regions. Locations on or around the Equator may have inferior coverage because the satellite's path does not directly fly horizontal to it only over it, and it's not helped by the Equator having the widest point to point circumference globally. The sweet spot appears to be the lines of the tropics of Cancer and Capricorn, as well as several degrees north and south. However, coverage will definitely improve by having more satellites in orbit.

As it stands, the Starlink satellites are placed in a lower vertical orbit than some of the more longstanding and traditional satellites that have been circling the planet for years. I've read that they are positioned 550km up, which doesn't really seem like a lot. This means that uplink capability is faster because the distance it has to travel to you on the ground is less.

l: Satellite dish placement and line of sight
p: When installing your satellite dish, it is important to have a good understanding of your installation location, vs the satellite trajectory, the point of the horizon and if there are any obscuring objects such as other houses, trees etc which are in the way of your line of sight to the horizon, relative to where the dish is placed.

Living on a hill with a 360° radial view would be the ultimate location however its also kind of rare. Conversely, living within a steep sided valley won't help your cause either. In the Outback of Australia, I'm certain that location will make an ideal spot to set up a Starlink dish. Does this mean that Australian city folk are going to migrate to Alice Springs, Mt Isa and Broken Hill? I hope not.. Lol.

This is a similar sort of exercise to putting solar panels up on your roof and trying to obtain the maximum amount of sunshine to hit your panels. The only difference is that satellites operate 24-hours a day so your placement isn't based on sunlight but the maximum clear line of sight to the horizon point before the satellite disappears off your radar. Assuming of course that another satellite is following in its path to continue your uplink connection.

If you live in the Northern Hemisphere, point your dish north facing, and in the Southern Hemisphere point south. Because that is the direction in which the satellites are travelling. If a professional is doing this for you they should already be aware of this configuration detail.

Well for starters, the access speed for downloading and uploading is incredibly fast. Many of you won't know what do with yourselves, considering the third world status of Australia's Internet malaise.

Setting up a Starlink dish is similar to setting up a Foxtel dish. You probably need to determine where in your house you're going to have your Starlink peripherals located and of course the appropriate cabling to go from them, through the house and back up to the roof. For that you'll need a professional installer to do it for you, like a cabler, builder or electrician. If you live in an apartment or a leased premises, this will be an issue.

As far as the Starlink kit itself is concerned, you don't actually get a lot. You get the dish which is quite large, some mounting brackets, a power supply (this thing does require a bit of juice, upward of 90 watts) and a modem, which is connected to your existing home network's router. Depending on how good you are in terms of configuring your router, you may actually be able to combine the speeds of Starlink with your existing service, let's say NBN if you're in Australia, to maximize the speed potential of your connection to the house. Apparently it is possible, but I'm thinking that once people have got Starlink up and running they will sever their NBN connection, and good point too, why would you bother paying for two services?

From what I've seen, the Starlink modem looks to be very lightweight and flimsy, and very narrow when standing up. It won't take a lot to knock it over. It probably needs some plastic feet or stabilisers, like what you see on Netgear routers to keep it upright. A note for Starlink's design team, please take this suggestion onboard.

Mobility - Starlink is not like Mobile WiFi at present. That is, you can't take it on the road with you. And this makes sense as the satellite dish would constantly need recalibration to retain an uplink. However, I am certain that this will be overcome in the next few years or less, mainly because Tesla are soon to roll out their forthcoming Tesla Model Pi smartphone which will have a satellite connection to the Starlink service built into the phone. Devices connecting to Starlink while on the move is something consumers will be screaming out for. Look on YouTube for more about the Tesla Model Pi.

Political Interference - Countries such as China, Iran, Afghanistan and Belarus would obviously frown upon disrupter technology like Starlink to bypass Orwellian control over their population. Other than deliberately shooting down satellites from ground based artillery and causing international outrage in the process, or deliberately cutting off the supply of Starlink kits to customers and revoking any license to Space X/Starlink, these countries will surely get their heckles up regardless.

Satellite Orbiting Overcrowding - Is this going to be an issue? The Astronomy Community seems to think so. They say that the reflective light off satellites as they orbit will severely impact the vision quality of viewing the night sky for deep space objects. This is something to follow up on, and whether or not it escalates to a point where something needs to be done about it.

Securing the Starlink service operates much like a crowd funding exercise. You pay an upfront deposit (in the US it's USD$100, in Australia it's A$150). You then sit in the queue. A few weeks out from delivery, you'll be asked to pay the remainder for your install equipment/kit, which could be anywhere in the region of $500 upward.

The ongoing monthly cost is expected to be USD$100, in Australia it will be around A$130, though prices are expected to change as it does with most monthly plans operated by telcos to try and induce business.

Starlink's arrival is for me, a welcome addition. For far too long I've had to put up with an inadequate service and pay an extraordinary cost for it, which is akin to daylight robbery. As stated above, Australia, where I live, truly operates on a third world network when it comes to the Internet. Some of the clowns that are operating the telecommunications policy in this country really need to join the circus. They are utterly hopeless. It takes a disrupter to come along and put the fear of death into them, knowing their current business model is about to head the way of the Dodo. Goodbye and good riddance.
